title: Rare Events Become Inevitable at Scale
concise_statement: Extremely unlikely events occur regularly when enough people, time, and opportunities exist.
detailed_explanation: Humans intuitively misunderstand probability at large scales. Events with tiny individual probabilities become statistically inevitable when repeated across massive populations and long time horizons.
implications: Shocking outcomes should often be expected statistically.
Tail events are normal features of large systems.
Probability intuition weakens at large scales.
Improbable does not mean impossible or suspicious.

title: Miracles Are Often Statistics Misunderstood
concise_statement: Events perceived as miraculous are frequently normal outcomes of large sample sizes.
detailed_explanation: Humans attribute extraordinary events to supernatural forces or fate because they underestimate how often rare events naturally occur in a world with billions of people and trillions of interactions.
implications: Avoid attributing randomness to hidden causes unnecessarily.
Statistical literacy improves judgment.
Extraordinary events require probabilistic interpretation.
Rare experiences are mathematically expected.

title: One-Hundred-Year Events Are Constantly Possible
concise_statement: Low-probability disasters become common when many independent risks exist simultaneously.
detailed_explanation: A one-percent annual probability event appears unlikely in isolation, but when numerous independent low-probability risks exist, the chance that at least one major disruption occurs becomes substantial.
implications: Expect periodic crises as normal.
Diversify against multiple risk categories.
Do not assume calm periods imply safety.
Complex systems naturally generate frequent disruptions.

title: Large Systems Amplify Extreme Outcomes
concise_statement: As population size and connectivity increase, the probability of impactful extreme behavior rises.
detailed_explanation: Larger and more interconnected societies create more opportunities for outlier individuals or events to influence global outcomes. Scale magnifies both innovation and disruption.
implications: Globalization increases exposure to systemic shocks.
Extreme individuals can disproportionately shape events.
Connectivity amplifies contagion effects.
Complexity increases unpredictability.

title: Media Selection Bias Creates Persistent Pessimism
concise_statement: News appears overwhelmingly negative because bad events are more attention-grabbing and statistically abundant globally.
detailed_explanation: Negative events attract more engagement than positive ones. As information systems globalize, the probability that some terrible event is occurring somewhere at any moment approaches certainty, creating a constant stream of alarming news.
implications: Media consumption can distort perception of reality.
Global awareness increases perceived instability.
Emotional pessimism may exceed objective conditions.
Attention economics favors negativity.

title: Expanded Horizons Increase Perceived Insecurity
concise_statement: The broader the scope of information people consume, the more vulnerable and uncertain the world feels.
detailed_explanation: Humans evolved in localized environments. Modern information systems expose individuals to global instability, creating psychological stress from events far outside personal influence or control.
implications: Global information overload can increase anxiety.
Psychological well-being may require limiting exposure.
Awareness does not necessarily improve control.
Modern insecurity is partly informational.

title: The World Always Contains Ongoing Chaos
concise_statement: Periods remembered as stable often contained substantial crises that are forgotten or overshadowed later.
detailed_explanation: Human memory simplifies history into narratives of calm or turmoil, but every era contains overlapping disruptions, recessions, conflicts, and shocks. Stability is often retrospective simplification.
implications: Nostalgia can distort historical understanding.
Crisis frequency is a persistent feature of reality.
Current instability is not historically unique.
Perceived disorder may partly reflect information visibility.

title: Humans Prefer Emotional Comfort Over Statistical Accuracy
concise_statement: People often seek confident explanations because uncertainty is psychologically painful.
detailed_explanation: Probabilistic thinking creates discomfort because it forces acceptance of ambiguity and lack of control. Confident predictions provide emotional relief even when accuracy is low.
implications: Overconfident experts gain disproportionate influence.
Nuanced communication is psychologically less persuasive.
False certainty can drive poor decisions.
Demand for prediction exceeds actual predictability.

title: Humans Resolve Doubt Prematurely
concise_statement: People are evolutionarily biased toward quickly eliminating uncertainty even when evidence is incomplete.
detailed_explanation: The human brain evolved to make rapid decisions under threat, favoring quick resolution over prolonged ambiguity. In modern complex environments, this tendency can produce overconfidence and poor judgment.
implications: People may adopt simplistic narratives prematurely.
Decision-making under uncertainty requires deliberate slowing down.
Intellectual humility is psychologically unnatural.
Markets and politics reward certainty signaling.

title: Authority Figures Satisfy the Need for Predictability
concise_statement: Experts gain influence partly because people crave the illusion of a controllable future.
detailed_explanation: Humans seek authoritative voices not only for information, but for psychological reassurance that the future can be understood and managed. Confidence often matters more socially than predictive accuracy.
implications: Forecasting industries persist despite weak accuracy.
People reward certainty over nuance.
Expert status can derive from confidence rather than competence.
Emotional reassurance is economically valuable.
